purpose: Levetiracetam is used to help prevent and control seizures in people with epilepsy. It can be used alone or together with other seizure medicines. Doctors may prescribe it for different types of seizures, including partial seizures, myoclonic seizures, and generalized tonic-clonic seizures.
how_it_works: Scientists believe levetiracetam works by calming down overexcited nerve signals in the brain that can trigger seizures. It attaches to a specific protein in the brain called SV2A, which helps regulate how brain cells communicate with each other. By doing this, it helps keep the brain's electrical activity more stable and reduces the chance of a seizure happening.
common_side_effects: Feeling tired or drowsy, dizziness, weakness, and headache are the most common side effects. Some people may also notice stuffy nose, sore throat, or loss of appetite. These effects are often mild and may improve after the first few weeks as your body adjusts.
warnings: Some people taking this medication may experience mood changes, irritability, anxiety, or depression — and in rare cases, thoughts of self-harm. It is very important to tell your doctor right away if you notice any changes in your mood or behavior. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first, as this can cause seizures to return or get worse.
typical_dosing: The usual starting dose for adults is 500 mg taken twice a day, once in the morning and once at night. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose over time, up to a maximum of 3000 mg per day, depending on how well it controls your seizures. Always take it exactly as your doctor prescribes, and try to take it at the same times each day.
